responses:
## Analysis

The current kernel is a 16-word unrolled loop followed by a branch tree that handles the remaining 0–15 words with constant indices. The bounds checks in the loop body are already eliminated, since `len(xs) >= 16` proves that `xs[0..15]` are valid. The tail tree is also already tight. Every previous attempt reordered or restructured the same branches and landed on exactly the same cost (3909), so further reordering of the tail is unlikely to help.

The remaining per-call overhead that scales with input length is the loop control: one length compare, one reslice (`xs = xs[16:]`), and the loop branch for every 16 words. Doubling the unroll factor for the main loop halves the number of those iterations. For long inputs, that removes a small but real fraction of the executed SSA instructions. Inputs shorter than 32 words skip the new loop entirely, so the tail behavior is unchanged for them.

This change is purely additive. It introduces no new indexing patterns, so correctness is preserved, and `xs` is still only resliced, never written.

## Proposed change

Add a 32-word unrolled loop ahead of the existing 16-word loop. The tail logic stays exactly as it is.

## Expected effect

- Long inputs: fewer loop-control instructions per word, so a modest cost reduction.
- Short inputs (under 32 words): the same path as before, plus one failed length check, so essentially no change.
- Correctness: unchanged, since the new loop covers exactly the words the 16-word loop would otherwise have covered and the tail is unmodified.

If this does not move the cost, the next thing to try is removing the `xs = xs[16:]` reslice in favor of a single index variable `i`, but that needs care because indexed access with a non-constant base can reintroduce bounds checks.
